IPLA under a log-Sobolev inequality

An entropy bound for the actual particle algorithm, derived through its scaled ULA representation.

Conditional Lean formalization. The particle scaling, entropy bounds, Gaussian-law identification, and parameter data processing are proved. The theorem assumes an LSI on the actual lifted target and explicit regular interpolation data from the shared ULA argument.

IPLA evolves one common parameter and a collection of latent particles. After rescaling the latent coordinates, the entire system is exactly an unadjusted Langevin algorithm on a larger Euclidean space. This page develops the resulting relative-entropy estimate under a log-Sobolev inequality (LSI) for that system's actual Gibbs target. The argument is assembled here from the repository's particle geometry and its shared ULA entropy proof; this page makes no claim that a separate published IPLA theorem has been reproduced.

The theorem is stated with all of its mathematical inputs. In particular, the LSI concerns the lifted target, and regular interpolation data supply the remaining density, weak-equation, and moment obligations of the ULA argument. The Lean development proves the entropy calculation and particle scaling from those inputs. Its conclusion measures convergence of the joint law to the Gibbs target in relative entropy.

Chapter 1The general theorem and its assumptions

Keep the LSI constant of the actual lifted target explicit. Its dependence on the particle count determines both the contraction rate and the allowable step.

1.1 · A bound for full joint relative entropy §

Let N>0N>0N>0, let dθ,dxd_\theta,d_xdθ​,dx​ be natural dimensions, and let U:Rdθ+dx→RU:\mathbb R^{d_\theta+d_x}\to\mathbb RU:Rdθ​+dx​→R be differentiable with LLL-Lipschitz gradient. Set D=dθ+NdxD=d_\theta+Nd_xD=dθ​+Ndx​. Below, ΠN\Pi_NΠN​ is the Gibbs probability measure of the scaled potential VNV_NVN​, μk\mu_kμk​ is the scaled IPLA state law, and

Hk=KL⁡(μk∥ΠN). H_k=\operatorname{KL}(\mu_k\Vert\Pi_N). Hk​=KL(μk​∥ΠN​).

Assume an initial probability law μ0\mu_0μ0​, an LSI on ΠN\Pi_NΠN​ with constant β>0\beta>0β>0, and

β≤NL,0<γ≤β4NL2. \beta\le NL,\qquad 0<\gamma\le\frac{\beta}{4NL^2}. β≤NL,0<γ≤4NL2β​.

Also supply RegularInterpolationData for potential VNV_NVN​, LSI constant β\betaβ, ULA step γ/N\gamma/Nγ/N, smoothness NLNLNL, and initialization μ0\mu_0μ0​. These analytic data are spelled out in Chapter 4. Then HkH_kHk​ is finite for every kkk, and the proved estimate is

Hk≤e−βγk/NH0+8γNDL2β. H_k\le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}H_0 +\frac{8\gamma ND L^2}{\beta}. Hk​≤e−βγk/NH0​+β8γNDL2​.

The positivity of LLL follows from β>0\beta>0β>0 and β≤NL\beta\le NLβ≤NL; it is not a missing division guard. The compatibility condition β≤NL\beta\le NLβ≤NL is an explicit input of the shared entropy argument. No strong-convexity assumption is used by this endpoint.

1.2 · Normalize the joint entropy by the number of particles §

Dividing the whole estimate by the positive particle number gives the intensive quantity H‾k=Hk/N\overline H_k=H_k/NHk​=Hk​/N:

H‾k≤e−βγk/NH‾0+8γDL2β. \overline H_k\le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}\overline H_0 +\frac{8\gamma D L^2}{\beta}. Hk​≤e−βγk/NH0​+β8γDL2​.

Both the initial contribution and the bias are divided by NNN. The theorem particle_kl_bound_normalized obtains this inequality from the full joint estimate; normalize_entropy_bound performs the scalar division and cancellation. Its use of a positive divisor preserves the inequality direction.

The normalization does not make this the parameter-marginal divergence. It remains the divergence of the entire state, divided by NNN. Chapter 7 gives the precise projection consequence and the factor needed to bound unscaled parameter KL. For fixed nonzero step, the displayed additive term allows persistent discretization error; the theorem does not assert that the Euler transition leaves ΠN\Pi_NΠN​ invariant.

Chapter 2The scaled state, target, and particle update

The reduction to ULA is an identity of potentials and Gaussian transitions. It is useful to work through the coordinates before substituting any entropy theorem.

2.1 · One parameter block and rescaled latent blocks §

Write the scaled state as z=(θ,z1,…,zN)z=(\theta,z^1,\ldots,z^N)z=(θ,z1,…,zN), with physical latent particles xi=N zix^i=\sqrt N\,z^ixi=N​zi. The Euclidean norm is the ordinary norm of these scaled coordinates. Define

VN(z)=∑i=1NU(θ,N zi),ΠN(dz)=ZN−1e−VN(z) dz. V_N(z)=\sum_{i=1}^N U(\theta,\sqrt N\,z^i),\qquad \Pi_N(dz)=Z_N^{-1}e^{-V_N(z)}\,dz. VN​(z)=i=1∑N​U(θ,N​zi),ΠN​(dz)=ZN−1​e−VN​(z)dz.

IPLA.potential is exactly this VNV_NVN​, and IPLA.gibbsTarget is exactly its normalized Gibbs expression. The parameter coordinate is unchanged by the rescaling. finrank_state proves that its real dimension is D=dθ+NdxD=d_\theta+Nd_xD=dθ​+Ndx​, allowing the shared ULA theorem's dimension parameter to be substituted without treating dθd_\thetadθ​ and dxd_xdx​ as equal.

Normalization is supplied in this theorem through IsLogSobolev, which includes that the target is a probability measure. The Gibbs expression alone would not prove that its partition function is positive and finite. No pair-target LSI is used to establish normalization or the lifted functional inequality.

2.2 · The Gaussian algorithm in original coordinates §

A ULA step for VNV_NVN​ with h=γ/Nh=\gamma/Nh=γ/N is

zk+1=zk−γN∇VN(zk)+2γN ξk,ξk∼N(0,ID). z_{k+1}=z_k-\frac\gamma N\nabla V_N(z_k) +\sqrt{\frac{2\gamma}{N}}\,\xi_k, \qquad\xi_k\sim\mathcal N(0,I_D). zk+1​=zk​−Nγ​∇VN​(zk​)+N2γ​​ξk​,ξk​∼N(0,ID​).

The parameter derivative of VNV_NVN​ is the sum of the pair parameter derivatives. Its iiith scaled latent derivative is N ∇xU(θ,Nzi)\sqrt N\,\nabla_x U(\theta,\sqrt N z^i)N​∇x​U(θ,N​zi). Thus the same step, after unscaling each latent block, reads

θk+1=θk−γN∑i=1N∇θU(θk,xki)+2γN ξkθ, \theta_{k+1}=\theta_k-\frac\gamma N\sum_{i=1}^N \nabla_\theta U(\theta_k,x_k^i) +\sqrt{\frac{2\gamma}{N}}\,\xi_k^\theta, θk+1​=θk​−Nγ​i=1∑N​∇θ​U(θk​,xki​)+N2γ​​ξkθ​, xk+1i=xki−γ∇xU(θk,xki)+2γ ξki. x_{k+1}^i=x_k^i-\gamma\nabla_x U(\theta_k,x_k^i) +\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\xi_k^i. xk+1i​=xki​−γ∇x​U(θk​,xki​)+2γ​ξki​.

scaledUpdate_parameter and scaledUpdate_particle prove these coordinate formulas, including the two different noise scales. The Gaussian coordinates and times are independent, and the entire noise sequence is independent of initialization. Those distributional assumptions appear explicitly in the noise-driven endpoint.

2.3 · Why the lifted smoothness is NL §

Let Jiz=(θ,Nzi)J_i z=(\theta,\sqrt N z^i)Ji​z=(θ,N​zi). The replicated pair maps satisfy the exact quadratic identity

∑i=1N∥Jiv∥2=N∥v∥2. \sum_{i=1}^N\|J_i v\|^2=N\|v\|^2. i=1∑N​∥Ji​v∥2=N∥v∥2.

Differentiating the finite sum gives ⟨∇VN(z),v⟩=∑i⟨∇U(Jiz),Jiv⟩ \langle\nabla V_N(z),v\rangle =\sum_i\langle\nabla U(J_i z),J_i v\rangle ⟨∇VN​(z),v⟩=∑i​⟨∇U(Ji​z),Ji​v⟩. Apply the base gradient's LLL-Lipschitz bound to a difference of two such expressions, then apply Cauchy–Schwarz to the particle sum. The quadratic identity on both arguments gives

∥∇VN(z)−∇VN(w)∥≤NL ∥z−w∥. \|\nabla V_N(z)-\nabla V_N(w)\| \le NL\,\|z-w\|. ∥∇VN​(z)−∇VN​(w)∥≤NL∥z−w∥.

The repository proves differentiability of VNV_NVN​ and this Lipschitz statement from the corresponding assumptions on UUU. The smoothness is therefore derived; the LSI constant β\betaβ is supplied separately. Keeping those roles distinct is essential because sharing the parameter across all pair terms prevents a direct independent-product tensorization argument.

For clarity, the quadratic identity follows directly from the coordinates: each pair norm contributes the same ∥vθ∥2\|v_\theta\|^2∥vθ​∥2, while its latent block contributes N∥vi∥2N\|v_i\|^2N∥vi​∥2. Summing gives N∥vθ∥2+N∑i∥vi∥2=N∥v∥2N\|v_\theta\|^2+N\sum_i\|v_i\|^2=N\|v\|^2N∥vθ​∥2+N∑i​∥vi​∥2=N∥v∥2. In the gradient comparison the particle sum is bounded by

L(∑i∥Ji(z−w)∥2)1/2(∑i∥Jiv∥2)1/2=NL∥z−w∥ ∥v∥. L\Big(\sum_i\|J_i(z-w)\|^2\Big)^{1/2} \Big(\sum_i\|J_i v\|^2\Big)^{1/2} =NL\|z-w\|\,\|v\|. L(i∑​∥Ji​(z−w)∥2)1/2(i∑​∥Ji​v∥2)1/2=NL∥z−w∥∥v∥.

Taking the supremum over unit test vectors gives the asserted Lipschitz constant. This also explains why using the unscaled particle coordinates would change the ambient metric and obscure the direct isotropic ULA representation.

Chapter 3The theorem concerns the actual Gaussian laws

There are two equivalent presentations of the algorithm: iteration of its measure transition, and a noise-driven recursion on a probability space. The development proves their law identity.

3.1 · Canonical particle laws and probability preservation §

particleLaws U γ μ k is the kkk-fold iteration of the actual Gaussian ULA law step for VNV_NVN​ at time γ/N\gamma/Nγ/N, beginning with μ\muμ. At k=0k=0k=0 it is exactly μ\muμ. Each transition pushes the independent product of the current law and the standard DDD-dimensional Gaussian through the displayed Euler update.

Gradient Lipschitzness gives the measurability needed for pushforward probability preservation. Consequently all of the particle laws are probability measures whenever initialization is a probability measure. This construction takes an initial measure directly and does not require choosing a particular probability space or Gaussian sequence to state the canonical entropy theorem.

The law identity also keeps the interpolation endpoint precise: a frozen-drift Gaussian interpolation started at μk\mu_kμk​ has law μk\mu_kμk​ at time zero and μk+1\mu_{k+1}μk+1​ at time h=γ/Nh=\gamma/Nh=γ/N. These endpoint identities are used when a continuous-time entropy comparison becomes a discrete one-step recurrence.

3.2 · Identify the existing IPLA implementation §

The original IPLA.laws follows an L2L^2L2 random initialization and an L2L^2L2 noise sequence. GaussianInnovations states that each scalar noise coordinate has law N(0,1)\mathcal N(0,1)N(0,1), that all coordinates across all times are independent, and that the noise sequence is independent of initialization. It does not silently replace arbitrary noise by Gaussian noise.

particleLaws_eq_laws proves that the canonical law at every step is the law of this recursion. Substitution into the canonical entropy estimates gives gaussian_ipla_kl_bound_normalized and its linear-LSI specialization. These corollaries retain the exact distributional assumptions and the same interpolation data, now initialized with the pushforward law of the random initial state.

This distinction lets a theorem about arbitrary initial probability measures coexist with the implementation's L2L^2L2 interface. Neither version assumes a Gaussian initial state. The regular density requirements of the interpolation data do, however, restrict which initial laws currently satisfy the conditional theorem.

Chapter 4The analytic assumptions behind the shared entropy argument

The new particle proof reuses a single explicit interface. Packaging its fields shortens the endpoint signature while keeping every remaining analytic obligation inspectable.

4.1 · Relative-density LSI and regular interpolation data §

Write ν=ΠN\nu=\Pi_Nν=ΠN​, ℓ=NL\ell=NLℓ=NL, and h=γ/Nh=\gamma/Nh=γ/N. The LSI normalization is

2βKL⁡(rν∥ν)≤∫∥∇log⁡r∥2 d(rν). 2\beta\operatorname{KL}(r\nu\Vert\nu) \le \int\|\nabla\log r\|^2\,d(r\nu). 2βKL(rν∥ν)≤∫∥∇logr∥2d(rν).

IsLogSobolev applies this inequality to strictly positive C1C^1C1 relative densities defining probability measures. Its convention agrees with the shared ULA entropy calculation. Extension to every density by approximation is not asserted by this definition.

RegularInterpolationData V_N β h ℓ μ supplies functions rk(t,z)r_k(t,z)rk​(t,z), time derivatives r˙k(t,z)\dot r_k(t,z)r˙k​(t,z), and error fields ek(t,z)e_k(t,z)ek​(t,z). On 0≤t≤h0\le t\le h0≤t≤h, it identifies rk(t)νr_k(t)\nurk​(t)ν with the actual frozen-drift Gaussian law begun at step kkk, requires strict positivity and spatial C1C^1C1 regularity, and supplies LocalEntropyRegularity. That local condition contains integrable domination for differentiating rlog⁡rr\log rrlogr, pointwise time derivatives, and measurability.

The structure additionally requires integrability of the squared relative score and error energy, and measurability of their cross term. It also supplies the admissible weak equation for 0≤t<h0\le t<h0≤t<h, the error-energy bound, and a squared-gradient moment bound at the start of every step. Integrability of the cross term is then derived from those energy assumptions by Young’s inequality. The structure contains no entropy recurrence or convergence conclusion. Its local regularity currently uses full time neighborhoods, including at zero.

4.2 · From the weak equation to entropy production §

The weak equation is an identity for every C1C^1C1 test function ψ\psiψ whose three displayed integrands are integrable:

∫r˙ ψ dν=−∫⟨∇r,∇ψ⟩ dν+∫r⟨e,∇ψ⟩ dν. \int\dot r\,\psi\,d\nu =-\int\langle\nabla r,\nabla\psi\rangle\,d\nu +\int r\langle e,\nabla\psi\rangle\,d\nu. ∫r˙ψdν=−∫⟨∇r,∇ψ⟩dν+∫r⟨e,∇ψ⟩dν.

The positive sign in its last term fixes the convention for eee. For a frozen drift, the intended field is e(z)=∇VN(z)−E[∇VN(X0)∣Xt=z]e(z)=\nabla V_N(z)-\mathbb E[\nabla V_N(X_0)\mid X_t=z]e(z)=∇VN​(z)−E[∇VN​(X0​)∣Xt​=z]. Constructing such a field and proving this admissible identity is an input to the current interface.

Local domination justifies differentiation under the entropy integral. Test the weak identity with 1+log⁡r1+\log r1+logr, use ∇r=r∇log⁡r\nabla r=r\nabla\log r∇r=r∇logr, and apply Young's inequality ⟨e,s⟩≤∥s∥2/4+∥e∥2\langle e,s\rangle\le\|s\|^2/4+\|e\|^2⟨e,s⟩≤∥s∥2/4+∥e∥2. With J(t)=∫∥∇log⁡r∥2d(rν)J(t)=\int\|\nabla\log r\|^2d(r\nu)J(t)=∫∥∇logr∥2d(rν), the formalized calculus gives

H′(t)≤−34J(t)+∫r(t,z)∥e(t,z)∥2 ν(dz). H'(t)\le-\tfrac34 J(t)+\int r(t,z)\|e(t,z)\|^2\,\nu(dz). H′(t)≤−43​J(t)+∫r(t,z)∥e(t,z)∥2ν(dz).

This derivative estimate is proved from the structure's analytic fields. The entropy derivative itself is not a field of the structure.

4.3 · The two energy estimates and finite entropy §

Let Gk=∫∥∇VN∥2dμkG_k=\int\lVert\nabla V_N\rVert^2d\mu_kGk​=∫∥∇VN​∥2dμk​, with its integrability required explicitly. The remaining quantitative fields are

∫rk(t)∥ek(t)∥2dν≤t2ℓ2Gk+2tDℓ2,Gk≤4ℓ2βHk+2Dℓ. \int r_k(t)\lVert e_k(t)\rVert^2d\nu \le t^2\ell^2G_k+2tD\ell^2, \qquad G_k\le\frac{4\ell^2}{\beta}H_k+2D\ell. ∫rk​(t)∥ek​(t)∥2dν≤t2ℓ2Gk​+2tDℓ2,Gk​≤β4ℓ2​Hk​+2Dℓ.

The first is the drift-error energy estimate suggested by Gaussian displacement moments and Lipschitzness. The shared ULA files prove the joint Gaussian displacement formula. Connecting that joint bound to an error field in the weak equation remains part of constructing the supplied data. The second gradient-moment comparison is also an explicit field; the endpoint does not derive it solely from the stated LSI.

The data's integrable entropy density proves finite extended KL. kl_finite and particle_kl_finite establish this fact before any real-valued bound is used. This matters because ENNReal.toReal sends infinity to zero. Here each displayed HkH_kHk​ really represents a finite KL divergence. kl_bound then assembles the proved calculus, LSI, scalar comparison, and iteration.

The Gaussian calculation uses the independent joint law of X0X_0X0​ and standard ZZZ, with Xt=X0−t∇VN(X0)+2tZX_t=X_0-t\nabla V_N(X_0)+\sqrt{2t}ZXt​=X0​−t∇VN​(X0​)+2t​Z. Vanishing Gaussian mean cancels its cross term, giving

E∥Xt−X0∥2=t2Gk+2tD. \mathbb E\|X_t-X_0\|^2=t^2G_k+2tD. E∥Xt​−X0​∥2=t2Gk​+2tD.

Lipschitzness bounds the joint squared drift difference by ℓ2E∥Xt−X0∥2\ell^2\mathbb E\|X_t-X_0\|^2ℓ2E∥Xt​−X0​∥2. To obtain the stated field-energy bound, a conditional drift representation must also connect this joint law to the weak equation; the density interface requests that resulting bound explicitly. This prevents an unproved passage between a joint expectation and a conditional vector field from being hidden inside notation.

Chapter 5Derive the recurrence, then substitute particle scales

The analytic proof is performed once for ULA. The particle argument changes the potential, time scale, smoothness constant, and dimension, then rewrites the resulting constants exactly.

5.1 · LSI absorbs the frozen-drift error §

Combine the production estimate with 2βH(t)≤J(t)2\beta H(t)\le J(t)2βH(t)≤J(t). For 0≤t<h0\le t<h0≤t<h, this gives

H′(t)≤−32βH(t)+t2ℓ2Gk+2tDℓ2. H'(t)\le-\tfrac32\beta H(t)+t^2\ell^2G_k+2tD\ell^2. H′(t)≤−23​βH(t)+t2ℓ2Gk​+2tDℓ2.

The numerical assumptions h≤β/(4ℓ2)h\le\beta/(4\ell^2)h≤β/(4ℓ2) and β≤ℓ\beta\le\ellβ≤ℓ imply hℓ≤1/4h\ell\le1/4hℓ≤1/4 and βh≤1/4\beta h\le1/4βh≤1/4. The shared proof bounds the forcing uniformly using Gk≤AG_k\le AGk​≤A, where A=(4ℓ2/β)Hk+2DℓA=(4\ell^2/\beta)H_k+2D\ellA=(4ℓ2/β)Hk​+2Dℓ. It obtains

H′(t)≤−32βH(t)+b,b=β4Hk+52hDℓ2. H'(t)\le-\tfrac32\beta H(t)+b, \qquad b=\tfrac\beta4 H_k+\tfrac52 hD\ell^2. H′(t)≤−23​βH(t)+b,b=4β​Hk​+25​hDℓ2.

An affine differential comparison bounds its forcing contribution by bhbhbh. The elementary estimate e−3x/2+x/4≤e−xe^{-3x/2}+x/4\le e^{-x}e−3x/2+x/4≤e−x, valid for 0≤x≤1/40\le x\le1/40≤x≤1/4, absorbs the HkH_kHk​ contribution at x=βhx=\beta hx=βh. Relaxing the remaining coefficient 5/2≤65/2\le65/2≤6 yields

Hk+1≤e−βhHk+6h2Dℓ2. H_{k+1}\le e^{-\beta h}H_k+6h^2D\ell^2. Hk+1​≤e−βhHk​+6h2Dℓ2.

RegularInterpolationData.one_step derives this recurrence from the data; it does not take the recurrence as an assumption.

The uniform-forcing bound has two parts. First, h2ℓ2(4ℓ2/β)≤β/4h^2\ell^2(4\ell^2/\beta)\le\beta/4h2ℓ2(4ℓ2/β)≤β/4, since hℓ2≤β/4h\ell^2\le\beta/4hℓ2≤β/4. Second, 2h2Dℓ3≤hDℓ2/22h^2D\ell^3\le hD\ell^2/22h2Dℓ3≤hDℓ2/2, since hℓ≤1/4h\ell\le1/4hℓ≤1/4. Add the original noise term 2hDℓ22hD\ell^22hDℓ2 to obtain the coefficient 5/25/25/2 in bbb. Nonnegativity of HkH_kHk​ and the dimension justifies these multiplications. Integrating the affine comparison then controls the forcing by bhbhbh, and the exponential-gap inequality absorbs its initial-entropy contribution with the correct sign. These are quantitative deductions from the step regime, rather than additional assumptions on the entropy path.

5.2 · The IPLA step restriction and forcing constant §

The ULA step restriction is transformed by positive-denominator algebra:

γN≤β4(NL)2⟺γ≤β4NL2. \frac\gamma N\le\frac\beta{4(NL)^2} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \gamma\le\frac\beta{4NL^2}. Nγ​≤4(NL)2β​⟺γ≤4NL2β​.

The one-step forcing transforms as

6(γN)2D(NL)2=6γ2DL2. 6\left(\frac\gamma N\right)^2D(NL)^2 =6\gamma^2DL^2. 6(Nγ​)2D(NL)2=6γ2DL2.

Thus the actual joint laws obey Hk+1≤e−βγ/NHk+6γ2DL2H_{k+1}\le e^{-\beta\gamma/N}H_k+6\gamma^2DL^2Hk+1​≤e−βγ/NHk​+6γ2DL2. Dividing by NNN gives

H‾k+1≤e−βγ/NH‾k+6γ2DL2N. \overline H_{k+1}\le e^{-\beta\gamma/N}\overline H_k +\frac{6\gamma^2DL^2}{N}. Hk+1​≤e−βγ/NHk​+N6γ2DL2​.

The main one-step theorems derive both statements from the interpolation data. The separate scalar helper normalize_lifted_entropy_recurrence expresses only the algebra of normalization and accordingly takes a recurrence as its explicit premise. Keeping that helper distinct from the main theorem makes clear where the analytic recurrence is proved.

5.3 · The constants 6 and 8 after iteration §

For q=e−βhq=e^{-\beta h}q=e−βh, repeated substitution gives the finite-horizon estimate

Hk≤qkH0+6h2Dℓ2∑j=0k−1qj. H_k\le q^kH_0+6h^2D\ell^2\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}q^j. Hk​≤qkH0​+6h2Dℓ2j=0∑k−1​qj.

The shared discrete proof retains this geometric-sum version. Since 0<βh≤1/40<\beta h\le1/40<βh≤1/4, the bound 1−e−βh≥3βh/41-e^{-\beta h}\ge3\beta h/41−e−βh≥3βh/4 controls the sum by 4/(3βh)4/(3\beta h)4/(3βh), producing 8hDℓ2/β8hD\ell^2/\beta8hDℓ2/β. The substitution into the resulting envelope is exact:

e−βhk=e−βγk/N,8hDℓ2β=8γNDL2β. e^{-\beta hk}=e^{-\beta\gamma k/N},\qquad \frac{8hD\ell^2}{\beta}=\frac{8\gamma ND L^2}{\beta}. e−βhk=e−βγk/N,β8hDℓ2​=β8γNDL2​.

lifted_entropy_rate_eq and lifted_entropy_bias_eq record those identities. normalized_entropy_bias_eq cancels the remaining divisor NNN when full joint entropy is normalized. The term 888 is therefore the shared ULA envelope constant, while the powers of NNN come entirely from the proved particle scaling.

Chapter 6The additional regime β = Nα

This useful specialization assumes an LSI of strength NαN\alphaNα for the actual lifted target. It is a conditional regime of the theorem, not an inference from an LSI for one parameter/latent pair.

6.1 · Compatibility, step size, and contraction rate §

Suppose α>0\alpha>0α>0, α≤L\alpha\le Lα≤L, and the supplied LSI for ΠN\Pi_NΠN​ has constant β=Nα\beta=N\alphaβ=Nα. Then

Nα≤NL ⟺ α≤L,γ≤Nα4NL2 ⟺ γ≤α4L2. N\alpha\le NL\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \alpha\le L, \qquad \gamma\le\frac{N\alpha}{4NL^2} \ \Longleftrightarrow\ \gamma\le\frac\alpha{4L^2}. Nα≤NL ⟺ α≤L,γ≤4NL2Nα​ ⟺ γ≤4L2α​.

The exponent also simplifies: e−(Nα)γk/N=e−αγke^{-(N\alpha)\gamma k/N}=e^{-\alpha\gamma k}e−(Nα)γk/N=e−αγk. The scaling module proves both the comparison equivalence and its forward implication, the step equivalence, and two rate identities matching the general and original ULA forms. These helpers require N>0N>0N>0 where cancellation occurs.

The effective rate per algorithmic step is now independent of NNN. This observation depends on the actual lifted LSI scaling linearly with NNN; if only a fixed lower bound on β\betaβ is available, the general theorem retains rate βγ/N\beta\gamma/Nβγ/N and its more restrictive step regime. The general result is therefore the primary statement.

6.2 · The intensive dimension and specialized entropy estimate §

The same substitution rewrites the normalized bias using

DN=dx+dθN,8γDL2Nα=8γL2α(dx+dθN). \frac DN=d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N},\qquad \frac{8\gamma DL^2}{N\alpha} =\frac{8\gamma L^2}{\alpha} \left(d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}\right). ND​=dx​+Ndθ​​,Nα8γDL2​=α8γL2​(dx​+Ndθ​​).

The resulting theorem is

H‾k≤e−αγkH‾0+8γL2α(dx+dθN). \overline H_k\le e^{-\alpha\gamma k}\overline H_0 +\frac{8\gamma L^2}{\alpha} \left(d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}\right). Hk​≤e−αγkH0​+α8γL2​(dx​+Ndθ​​).

For the one-step version, dividing the forcing by NNN similarly gives 6γ2L2(dx+dθ/N)6\gamma^2L^2(d_x+d_\theta/N)6γ2L2(dx​+dθ​/N). The scaling module records this identity and the corresponding normalized recurrence. particle_kl_bound_of_linear_lsi proves the displayed final bound by specializing the general theorem; the Gaussian implementation corollary follows through the law identity shown earlier.

At fixed latent dimension, the latent contribution in this bound persists as NNN grows. The decreasing parameter-dimension contribution dθ/Nd_\theta/Ndθ​/N is a feature of normalized joint entropy. It is not itself a bound on unscaled parameter entropy or distance to an optimizer.

Chapter 7What follows for the parameter marginal

Projection gives an immediate entropy consequence about a genuine parameter distribution. Its reference measure is the parameter projection of the same lifted Gibbs target.

7.1 · Define the target and use extended KL data processing §

Let pθ(z)=θp_\theta(z)=\thetapθ​(z)=θ, let μkθ=(pθ)#μk\mu_k^\theta=(p_\theta)_\#\mu_kμkθ​=(pθ​)#​μk​, and define ΠNθ=(pθ)#ΠN\Pi_N^\theta=(p_\theta)_\#\Pi_NΠNθ​=(pθ​)#​ΠN​. The definition parameterTarget uses this exact pushforward, with no need to prove a formula for a marginal density.

The projection is continuous and measurable, so pushing forward any probability law preserves its mass. The module proves this for arbitrary state laws and for the actual Gibbs target. Mathlib's KL data-processing inequality then yields the extended-valued estimate

KL⁡(μkθ∥ΠNθ)≤KL⁡(μk∥ΠN). \operatorname{KL}(\mu_k^\theta\Vert\Pi_N^\theta) \le\operatorname{KL}(\mu_k\Vert\Pi_N). KL(μkθ​∥ΠNθ​)≤KL(μk​∥ΠN​).

parameter_kl_le_joint is generic in both state measures, while parameter_kl_le_gibbs_joint specializes its target. No concentration assumption is needed for this measure-theoretic inequality. It compares the sampled parameter law to a probability distribution rather than to a selected point.

At an informal density level, data processing is Jensen's inequality for the convex function u↦ulog⁡uu\mapsto u\log uu↦ulogu: averaging a joint relative density over coordinates that are then forgotten cannot increase its entropy. The formal proof invokes the measure-theoretic theorem directly, so it also applies when no convenient conditional or marginal density formula has been constructed. Only measurability of the projection and the probability hypotheses are needed for the extended-valued comparison; finiteness enters when a real-valued inequality is requested in the next step.

7.2 · Transfer finite bounds with the correct factor §

The finite joint KL proved earlier implies finite parameter KL. The module establishes this in the extended nonnegative reals before converting either quantity to a real number. Its generic and Gibbs-specific finiteness lemmas support the real data-processing inequality and bound-transfer lemmas.

In particular, a full joint bound Hk≤BH_k\le BHk​≤B gives parameter KL at most BBB. A normalized bound Hk/N≤B‾H_k/N\le\overline BHk​/N≤B instead gives

KL⁡(μkθ∥ΠNθ)≤NB‾. \operatorname{KL}(\mu_k^\theta\Vert\Pi_N^\theta) \le N\overline B. KL(μkθ​∥ΠNθ​)≤NB.

parameter_kl_bound_of_per_particle_bound proves exactly this multiplication by the positive particle count. Omitting it would incorrectly identify normalized joint entropy with marginal entropy.

These conclusions do not bound error around a marginal-likelihood maximizer. Such a statement would additionally need a suitable concentration or optimization argument for ΠNθ\Pi_N^\thetaΠNθ​, and a way to connect the chosen discrepancy to that goal. Those further hypotheses and conclusions belong to a different theorem from the LSI entropy extension presented here.

The combined particle-law corollaries perform these transfers directly. In the general regime they prove

KL⁡(μkθ∥ΠNθ)≤e−βγk/NH0+8γNDL2β. \operatorname{KL}(\mu_k^\theta\Vert\Pi_N^\theta) \le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}H_0+\frac{8\gamma ND L^2}{\beta}. KL(μkθ​∥ΠNθ​)≤e−βγk/NH0​+β8γNDL2​.

Under the supplied lifted LSI of strength NαN\alphaNα, they prove the specialized bound

KL⁡(μkθ∥ΠNθ)≤N[e−αγkH0N+8γL2α(dx+dθN)]. \operatorname{KL}(\mu_k^\theta\Vert\Pi_N^\theta) \le N\left[e^{-\alpha\gamma k}\frac{H_0}{N} +\frac{8\gamma L^2}{\alpha}\left(d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}\right)\right]. KL(μkθ​∥ΠNθ​)≤N[e−αγkNH0​​+α8γL2​(dx​+Ndθ​​)].

The initialization on these right-hand sides remains the full joint divergence H0=KL⁡(μ0∥ΠN)H_0=\operatorname{KL}(\mu_0\Vert\Pi_N)H0​=KL(μ0​∥ΠN​). Data processing cannot replace it by the smaller initial parameter divergence in this argument. The finite-parameter theorem separately makes explicit that this is a finite divergence of the actual parameter law.

1import IPLA.Dynamics2import IPLA.ProductReference3import Mathlib.Probability.Independence.InfinitePi45set_option linter.style.header false67/-! # The canonical law of Gaussian IPLA89The coordinate laws and independence fields of `GaussianInnovations` determine10the entire noise-path law. Packing a single countable product of standard real11Gaussian coordinates avoids any assumed grouping of independent vector blocks.12Initialization is independent of that path by the existing algorithm hypothesis.13The actual IPLA output laws therefore depend only on the initialization law,14the potential, and the step size, irrespective of their probability realization.15-/1617noncomputable section18open MeasureTheory ProbabilityTheory19open scoped ENNReal NNReal2021namespace IPLA2223/-- A coordinate records the iteration and the parameter or particle block. -/24abbrev NoiseCoordinate (N dθ dx : ℕ) := ℕ × (Fin dθ ⊕ (Fin N × Fin dx))2526/-- The canonical scalar noise source: independent standard real Gaussians. -/27def canonicalFlatNoiseLaw (N dθ dx We define the usual infimum of12quadratic coupling costs here. The value lies in `ℝ≥0∞`, so a measure without13finite second moment cannot silently acquire distance zero by `toReal`.1415This file proves the passage from an actual pair of random variables to a16transport bound, and the L² perturbation estimate used in synchronous coupling.17It does not assert existence or invariance of a Langevin diffusion.18-/1920noncomputable section2122open MeasureTheory23open scoped ENNReal NNReal2425namespace ULA2627variable {H : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup H] [MeasurableSpace H]28  [BorelSpace H] [SecondCountableTopology H]2930/-- A joint measure whose two marginals are the specified measures. -/31structure Coupling (μ ν : Measure H) where32  joint : Measure (H × H)33  fst : joint.map Prod.fst = μ34  snd : joint.map Prod.snd = ν3536/-- The square root of the quadratic transport cost of a joint measure. -/37def couplingCost (γ : Measure (H × H)) : ℝ≥0∞ :=38  eLpNorm (fun p : H × H ↦ p.1 - p.2) 2 γ3940/-- Wasserstein-2 as the infimum over every coupling, with infinite costs retained. -/41def wasserstein2 (μ ν : Measure H) : ℝ≥0∞ :=42  ⨅ c : Coupling μ ν, couplingCost c.joint4344/-- The real-valued distance, used only after a finite-cost coupling has been45provided. Results below carry that finiteness obligation explicitly. -/46def wasserstein2Real (μ ν : Measure H) : ℝ := (wasserstein2 μ ν).toReal4748omit [BorelSpace H] [SecondCountableTopology H] in49/-- Any particular coupling gives an upper bound on Wasserstein-2. -/50theorem wasserstein2_le_couplingCost {μ ν : Measure H} (c : Coupling μ ν) :51    wasserstein2 μ ν ≤ couplingCost c.joint :=52  iInf_le _ c5354variable {Ω : Type*} [MeasurableSpace Ω] (P : Measure Ω)5556/-- A pair of random variables supplies a coupling of their laws. -/57def randomVariableCoupling (X Y : Ω → H) (hX : Measurable X) (hY : Measurable Y) :58    Coupling (P.map X) (P.map Y) where59  joint := P.map (fun ω ↦ (X ω, Y ω))60  fst := by61    rw [Measure.map_map measurable_fst (hX.prodMk hY)]62    rfl63  snd := by64    rw [Measure.map_map measurable_snd (hX.prodMk hY)]65    rfl6667/-- The same construction for almost-everywhere measurable representatives. -/68def aeRandomVariableCoupling (X Y : Ω → H)69    (hX : AEMeasurable X P) (hY : AEMeasurable Y P) :70    Coupling (P.map X) (P.map Y) where71  joint := P.map (fun ω ↦ (X ω, Y ω))72  fst := by73    rw [AEMeasurable.map_map_of_aemeasurable measurable_fst.aemeasurable (hX.prodMk hY)]74    rfl75  snd := by76    rw [AEMeasurable.map_map_of_aemeasurable measurable_snd.aemeasurable (hX.prodMk hY)]77    rfl7879/-- The transport cost of a random-variable coupling is its L² distance. -/80theorem randomVariableCoupling_cost (X Y : Ω → H)81    (hX : Measurable X) (hY : Measurable Y) :82    couplingCost (randomVariableCoupling P X Y hX hY).joint =83      eLpNorm (fun ω ↦ X ω - Y ω) 2 P := by84  unfold couplingCost randomVariableCoupling85  exact eLpNorm_map_measure86    (by fun_prop) (hX.prodMk hY).aemeasurable8788/-- An actual coupling bounds the Wasserstein distance between the two laws. -/89theorem wasserstein2_le_random_cost (X Y : Ω → H)90    (hX : Measurable X) (hY : Measurable Y) :91    wasserstein2 (P.map X) (P.map Y) ≤ eLpNorm (fun ω ↦ X ω - Y ω) 2 P := by92  simpa only [randomVariableCoupling_cost] using93    wasserstein2_le_couplingCost (randomVariableCoupling P X Y hX hY)9495/-- Almost-everywhere measurability suffices for the random-variable bound. -/96theorem wasserstein2_le_ae_random_cost (X Y : Ω → H)97    (hX : AEMeasurable X P) (hY : AEMeasurable Y P) :98    wasserstein2 (P.map X) (P.map Y) ≤ eLpNorm (fun ω ↦ X ω - Y ω) 2 P := by99  refine (wasserstein2_le_couplingCost (aeRandomVariableCoupling P X Y hX hY)).trans_eq ?_100  exact eLpNorm_map_measure (by fun_prop) (hX.prodMk hY)101102/-- A finite L² coupling permits conversion to the usual real-valued bound. -/103theorem wasserstein2_le_random_cost_real (X Y : Ω → H)104    (hX : Measurable X) (hY : Measurable Y)105    (hXY : MemLp (fun ω ↦ X ω - Y ω) 2 P) :106    wasserstein2Real (P.map X) (P.map Y) ≤107      (eLpNorm (fun ω ↦ X ω - Y ω) 2 P).toReal :=108  ENNReal.toReal_mono hXY.eLpNorm_ne_top (wasserstein2_le_random_cost P X Y hX hY)109110/-- L² random variables provide a finite transport bound equal to their Banach111space distance. V ω)144    (hcontract : ∀ᵐ ω ∂P, ‖A ω‖ ≤ (q : ℝ) * ‖X ω - Y ω‖) :145    eLpNorm (fun ω ↦ X' ω - Y' ω) 2 P ≤146      (q : ℝ≥0∞) * eLpNorm (fun ω ↦ X ω - Y ω) 2 P + eLpNorm V 2 P := by147  rw [eLpNorm_congr_ae hidentity]148  exact (eLpNorm_sub_le (by norm_num : (1 : ℝ≥0∞) ≤ 2)).trans149    (add_le_add (eLpNorm_contraction P A (fun ω ↦ X ω - When it consists of independent standard9Gaussian vectors this definition is the unadjusted Langevin algorithm.10The algebraic coupling results apply to every common noise sequence.11-/1213noncomputable section1415open scoped NNReal1617namespace ULA1819/-- ULA iterates, with the initial condition and every noise vector visible. -/20def ulaChain {d : ℕ} (U : E d → ℝ) (h : ℝ) (initial : E d)21    (noise : ℕ → E d) : ℕ → E d22  | 0 => initial23  | n + 1 => ulaUpdate U h (ulaChain U h initial noise n) (noise n)2425@[simp] theorem ulaChain_zero {d : ℕ} (U : E d → ℝ) (h : ℝ)26    (initial : E d) (noise : ℕ → E d) : ulaChain U h initial noise 0 = initial := rfl2728@[simp] theorem ulaChain_succ {d : ℕ} (U : E d → ℝ) (h : ℝ)29    (initial : E d) (noise : ℕ → E d) (n : ℕ) :30    ulaChain U h initial noise (n + 1) =31      ulaUpdate U h (ulaChain U h initial noise n) (noise n) := rfl3233/-- Measurable initial data and noises give measurable iterates. -/34theorem ulaChain_measurable {Ω : Type*} [MeasurableSpace Ω] {d : ℕ}35    (U : E d → ℝ) (h : ℝ) (L : ℝ≥0)36    (hLip : LipschitzWith L (gradient U))37    (initial : Ω → E d) (noise : ℕ → Ω → E d)38    (hinitial : Measurable initial) (hnoise : ∀ n, Measurable (noise n)) (n : ℕ) :39    Measurable (fun ω ↦ ulaChain U h (initial ω) (fun k ↦ noise k ω) n) := by40  have hg : Measurable (gradient U) := hLip.continuous.measurable41  induction n with42  | zero => exact hinitial43  | succ n ih =>44      simp only [ulaChain_succ, ulaUpdate]45      exact (ih.sub ((hg.comp ih).const_smul h)).add46        ((hnoise n).const_smul (Real.sqrt (2 * h)))4748end ULA

1import UnadjustedLangevin.HilbertDalalyan2import UnadjustedLangevin.InitialExtension34set_option linter.style.header false56/-!7# Dalalyan's initial Wasserstein term on concrete product extensions89The reference diffusion may be realized separately for each initial coupling.10The sample space is always `(H × H) × S`, with probability measure11`c.joint.prod Q`.
